sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While search agents demonstrate impressive capabilities in multi-step question answering, their robustness to poor-quality evidence remains under-explored. Such evidence is rare in benchmark corpora, and resulting failures are hard to reproduce. We propose DeepStress, a dynamic stress-testing framework that subjects agents to degraded evidence at controlled rates. It replaces the retrieval module with a synthetic environment where documents are generated dynamically for each query, under independent control of their trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. To characterize behavior under stress, we go beyond binary accuracy with a five-way classification of final-answer outcomes and two new reliability-aware metrics, RAS and CoPRAS, which credit cautious behavior and account for computational cost. Evaluating 12 systems on questions from HotpotQA and BrowseComp-Plus, we find that several open-weight agents answer confidently when sources contain obvious credibility red flags, and that many HotpotQA questions are answered from parametric knowledge even when all returned documents are factually wrong.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), model first retrieves passages relevant to the user query, then conditions its answer on the retrieved evidence. Search agents extend this paradigm by making retrieval iterative: they interleave reasoning steps with calls to external search tools, gathering evidence before producing final answer. Their performance depends not only on the language model used for synthesis, but also on how evidence is retrieved, how reliable it is, and how the agent adapts its search and reasoning strategy to the evidence it receives. However, standard search-agent evaluations often reduce performance to final-answer accuracy, hiding qualitatively different failure modes such as poor retrieval, misleading 1 evidence, or ineffective search behavior. Recent work, such as BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025), decouples retriever and model performance by utilizing curated corpus where questions are paired with supportive and hard-negative documents. However, robustness failures are typically observed post-hoc, and the low-signal conditions are difficult to reproduce. Our study focuses on how search agents behave when the quality of retrieved evidence is explicitly controlled: we analyze fine-grained final-answer outcomes and complement them with exploratory analyses of search and reasoning behavior. Inspired by stress-testing methodologies, we introduce DeepStress, simulation environment designed to evaluate the robustness of deep search agents. Much like simulated environments used for autonomous vehicles, where extreme conditions are generated to test resilience, DeepStress places search agents in challenging scenarios where search results can be severely degraded. It intercepts the agents search calls and replaces the retrieval module with synthetic environment, allowing us to precisely manipulate the properties of the returned documents along three trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. axes: DeepStress is not replacement for existing benchmarks but acts as controlled laboratory for stress testing of search-agent behavior with the following contributions: 1. We introduce DeepStress, controlled simulation stress test environment that evaluates search agents dynamically on synthetic documents modified along three axes: trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. 2. We evaluate several agents across multiple experimental conditions and document substantial behavior differences when facing degraded documents and propose novel score called RAS (Reliability-Aware Score) that we evaluate against computational costs.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Search agents. Early work such as ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) and IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023) showed that off-the-shelf LLMs can be prompted to interleave reasoning with external actions or retrieval, enabling multi-step information seeking without task-specific training. More recent work trains search behavior directly. Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), for instance, uses reinforcement learning (RL) on multi-hop question-answering (QA) tasks, with rewards derived from final-answer correctness, to encourage models to issue useful search queries during reasoning. ZeroSearch (Sun et al., 2025) further removes the dependence on live search engine during training by using fine-tuned language model to generate documents that mimic search-engine outputs. parallel line of work targets deep-research agents, which produce longer, citation-rich answers over multiple rounds of retrieval and synthesis. DR-Tulu (Shao et al., 2026), for example, uses evolving rubrics as RL rewards to improve long-form research answers. These works focus on improving search-agent capabilities under given retrieval process. In contrast, our goal is to evaluate how search agents behave under controlled retrieval environment. Search benchmarks. Search agents are commonly evaluated on their ability to gather relevant evidence through iterative reasoning and search. Multi-hop QA datasets require models to locate and combine evidence about multiple entities before answering. HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) introduced diverse set of questions over Wikipedia entries, together with supporting sentence-level facts required for reasoning over the question. More recent benchmarks such as BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) introduce harder questions answerable through web browsing, where the answer is short and easily verifiable but difficult to find, requiring persistent search over entangled constraints. BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025) further improves experimental control by using fixed corpus with human-verified supporting documents and mined challenging negatives, allowing us to disentangle the retriever effect from that of the LLM. Our work follows this line of controlled evaluation, but isolates different factor: how agents react to changes in the quality of retrieved evidence. Adversarial environments. Recent work evaluates agents by perturbing the external observations they receive. AgentNoiseBench (Wang et al., 2026) directly replaces or corrupts tool outputs, while SafeSearch (Dong et al., 2026) and SearchGEO (Chen et al., 2026) expose search agents to controlled unreliable or manipulated search results. WARP (Zhang et al., 2026) poisons existing usergenerated web pages, exploiting their repeated retrieval by deep-research agents to steer their reports. Unlike these attack-oriented evaluations, DeepStress uses controlled semantic perturbations to study how search agents respond to changes in evidence trustworthiness, relevance, and factuality. Beyond final-answer accuracy. Search agents can fail in many different ways: an agent may give wrong answer, express uncertainty, fail to produce final answer, or exhaust its tool-call budget. Recent work on agent evaluation has argued for more detailed failure analysis, including taxonomies of reasoning, planning, tool-use, and system-execution errors (Deshpande et al., 2025). Beyond final outcomes, the trajectory itself is also informative, as highlighted by TRACE (Kim et al., 2026). Prior work has studied search trajectories through query reformulation and evidence reuse (Ning et al., 2026), and has shown that additional search calls can be helpful, wasteful, or harmful depending on retrieval conditions (Shi et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026). Our work combines these two views: we report fine-grained final-answer outcomes and analyze whether agents detect and verbalize degradations in retrieved documents. Robustness to knowledge conflict. By manipulating the quality of retrieved documents, our setting creates controlled cases where agents must reason from evidence that may be unreliable or conflicting, connecting our work to prior studies on knowledge conflict. DRAGged into Conflicts (Cattan et al., 2025) introduces taxonomy of conflict situations in RAG, together with the expected model behavior for each category. TRACK (Feng et al., 2026) studies how LLMs propagate newly provided facts through multi-step reasoning when these facts conflict with the models initial parametric knowledge. We differ from these studies by evaluating active search agents rather than static RAG or in-context reasoning pipelines. Instead of only asking whether model can resolve conflict once the evidence is given, we study how agents behave while searching under controlled degradations of the retrieved documents.

sections.title: 3.1 Simulation environment
sections.content: The core of the DeepStress methodology is to replace the standard search tool with simulated environment. Documents are dynamically generated for each agent query rather than precomputed, since different agents, or the same agent under different conditions, may follow different search trajectories for the same question. This ensures that each simulated search result is tailored to the agents actual query while preserving the controlled reliability attributes imposed by the scenario. Returning one controlled document per call differs from traditional retrieval settings, but is appropriate for our laboratory experiment, as it provides finer control over the evidence shown to the agent and isolates agent behavior from retrieval variability. (1) Let {D1, D2, . . . , Dn} be the set of dimensions under study. scenario γ specifies probability for each dimension, chosen by the experimenter: πγ = (cid:0)πγ(D1), . . . , πγ(Dn)(cid:1) For each simulated search call, we sample one binary label per dimension from the scenario probabilities. These labels define the target properties of the returned document. In the experiments reported in this paper, they are translated into dimensionspecific prompt instructions, although the framework itself is not tied to prompt-based generation. For example, if Dk corresponds to factuality and πγ(Dk) = 80%, then the document is sampled as factually correct with probability 80% and factually incorrect with probability 20%. In our implementation1, this label determines whether the dynamic prompt includes supporting evidence or factual errors, both for extreme values πγ(Dk) = 0% or 100% or more balanced situations.

sections.title: 3.2 Simulating document reliability
sections.content: In this paper, we focus on controlled experimental setup where we manipulate three source attributes: Trustworthiness (T): whether the source appears credible based on its style, structure and URL, regardless of its factuality; Relevance (R): whether the source meaningfully addresses the model-generated query rather than covering unrelated content; Factuality (F): whether the claims contained in the source are factually correct. 1The code for this flexible environment is publicly available and the repository link will be provided after peer-review. We generate documents with an LLM, using the sampled values of , R, and to control the output. For each search call, the simulator generates one synthetic document with title and URL; its length is chosen to approximate Wikipedia paragraph. The agents search query is passed to the LLM as the query the document should address, while the sampled labels are converted into dimensionspecific prompt instructions. Full prompt construction, generation details as well as document examples are provided in Appendix D.1. in Factually correct documents (F = 1), are evidence: dataset-provided grounded HotpotQA gold Wikipedia for paragraphs and human-verified evidence documents for BrowseComp-Plus. This reduces accidental errors on details such as dates or locations. Factually incorrect documents (F = 0) are generated with instructions to introduce severe factual errors. Trustworthy documents (T=1), are generated with plausible reliable URL and page title. For low-trust results (T=0), we sample domain from the OpenSources list2 of misleading and outright fake websites, generate plausible page title for that domain, and include specific instructions in the content generation prompt. Irrelevant documents (R=0), are generated by replacing the generation target with an unrelated question sampled from the dataset and use its associated supporting context. To mimic realistic partial web search, the query passed to the generator is document title sampled from that unrelated support context. This produces coherent and grounded document that is useful for another information need, but irrelevant to the original question asked to the agent.

sections.title: 4.1 Datasets
sections.content: We draw questions from two QA datasets that differ in both question difficulty and exposure to LLM pretraining. HotpotQA questions typically require few reasoning hops over Wikipedia passages and are answerable from small set of supporting paragraphs. BrowseComp-Plus, derived from BrowseComp, instead contains queries constructed by inversion from target entity under multiple constraints; answering them requires iterative search and aggregation across many documents, and stateof-the-art retrievers achieve low recall on its corpus of adversarially mined distractors. The two datasets are also complementary in their dependence on supporting documents. HotpotQA answers often involve general knowledge that models may store in their parameters, and the corpus itself has likely been seen during pretraining. By controlling the factuality of the supporting documents, we can therefore study how model handles conflicts between its parametric knowledge and the dynamic knowledge returned by search. BrowseComp-Plus questions, in contrast, cannot be answered without supporting documents, as the corpus is too recent to be known by current LLMs. With no such conflict, we can study instead how contradictory supporting documents affect the reasoning strategy of search agent. 4.2 Evaluated systems We have selected systems to cover diverse set of search-agent designs: closed-weight and openweight models, different model sizes, and different training procedures such as supervised finetuning and RL under different reward objectives. system denotes model together with its harness, i.e., the orchestration code and prompts that determine how context is assembled, how tools are invoked, and how model outputs are parsed. To keep the comparison controlled, simulated documents are formatted according to the conventions expected by each harness5. In total, twelve systems are evaluated. GPT systems (gpt-5-nano and gpt-5-mini), each run with low, medium, and high reasoning effort, provide six closed-weight tool-calling baselines. SpiqaDR6 is 3B Qwen2.5based search agent trained with RL for scientific literature search; detailed description is given in Appendix D.3. Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025) is 7B Qwen2.5-based search agent trained with RL to interleave reasoning with multi-turn search. AutoRefine (Shi et al., 2026) is 3B Qwen2.5based retrieval-augmented reasoning model that alternates search with explicit evidence-refinement steps before answering. ASearcher (Gao et al., 2026) is 7B Qwen2.5-based search agent trained with asynchronous RL for long-horizon information seeking; we use its local-RAG variant rather than the web-search version. DR-Tulu (Shao et al., 2026) is an 8B open deep-research model trained with RL and evolving rubrics to produce long-form, citation-grounded answers. We also evaluate DRTulu (no reasoning), which uses the same checkpoint with modified orchestration wrapper: whenever the model opens <think> block, the wrapper immediately closes it, preventing explicit reasoning while keeping the same tool-use and answer format.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We have introduced DeepStress, controlled simulation framework for stress-testing Deep Search agents under degraded evidence. Our experiments reveal substantial differences in agents robustness, uncertainty expression, and search adaptation, leading to three main conclusions. First, source reliability should be explicitly considered in the design of search agents, so that they can assess retrieved evidence and adapt their behavior accordingly. Second, robustness to conflicts between parametric knowledge and retrieved evidence should be systematically evaluated: producing correct answers despite consistently incorrect retrieved evidence may indicate robustness, but also benchmark contamination. Third, aggregate measures such as the proposed RAS metrics provide useful operational characterization of system performance by capturing robustness across different levels of evidence degradation. Finally, although our framework relies on synthetic interventions, the conditions it models reflect genuine deployment risks, as agents operating on the open Web can encounter erroneous or deliberately manipulated content (Zhang et al., 2026). Given these findings, we recommend integrating controlled stress testing into the evaluation framework for Deep Search systems. Two directions follow from this work. First, by examining query formulation and reasoning steps, we move toward process-based evaluation that complements outcome-level results with an analysis of agent search behavior and evidence integration. Second, DeepStress could also support the training of more robust agents. The brittleness of systems trained with narrow outcome-based rewards motivates reliability-aware training objectives, for which the controlled document labels and RAS could provide useful starting point. sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our simulator is designed as controlled environment for studying how document quality affects agent behavior. Each search call returns one generated document. This lets us control the evidence seen by the agent, but makes the search setting simpler than real search. In particular, we do not model cases where single search call returns several documents with conflicting, incomplete, or irrelevant content. We study simple search agents that use single search loop and one type of search tool. This helps isolate the effect of document quality and keeps the results easy to interpret. However, our findings mainly apply to this type of agent. They may not directly apply to more complex systems that use summarization, reranking, query reformulation, or sub-agents. We vary the three reliability dimensions independently and use LLM-generated documents. This gives us precise control over each dimension, but we do not study documents where several reliability issues appear at the same time. Synthetic documents may also be cleaner, less noisy, and less diverse than real search results. Our control experiments and human evaluation suggest that the setup is still useful for studying agent behavior, but these documents are not perfect substitute for real web content. Finally, our document generation pipeline requires each question to have supporting evidence. We use this evidence to ground factually correct documents, such as Wikipedia paragraphs from HotpotQA or reference documents from BrowseComp-Plus, and reduce hallucinations from the generator. Benchmarks without such evidence can still be used, but their factually correct documents may contain generator errors. This would make the factuality axis noisier and the conclusions less reliable.

sections.title: Ethical concerns
sections.content: This work is mainly dedicated to evaluation and diagnosis, and is intended to assess the behavior of models with respect to unreliable documents that could be retrieved by search engines. We believe that the subject of the study itself has significant impact towards trustworthy and explainable Artificial Intelligence. We are aware that for the sake of evaluation we generate unreliable synthetic documents, including untrustworthy and non-factual documents, but these documents are generated dynamically for the sake of the experiment and are not meant to be distributed. When presenting samples of such documents, we will systematically add warning notice mentioning that they contain unreliable content. We are however also aware that the methodology could be misused with the objective of generating such documents for illicit purposes. We will include disclaimer on the code repository discouraging such misuse. Regarding the human annotation process for evaluating the "quality" of synthetic documents (quality meaning here that they correspond to the purpose they were designed for), the annotators were internal colleagues that contributed on voluntary basis, and there was no specific compensation. Annotators were fully aware that they were likely to be exposed to unreliable documents.

sections.title: A Details about synthetically generated
sections.content: documents Synthetic document generation is central to our stress-testing setup. This section provides additional information about the quality of the generated documents, including human evaluation results, statistics, and examples. A.1 Human evaluation Hao Sun, Zile Qiao, Jiayan Guo, Xuanbo Fan, Yingyan Hou, Yong Jiang, Pengjun Xie, Yan Zhang, Fei To validate that our generation pipeline follows the intended document attributes, we conduct human evaluation with three annotators. The sample focuses on relevant documents: in our generation pipeline, relevance is controlled systematically by swapping the agent query, whereas the LLM is mainly responsible for following the trustworthiness and factuality constraints. Annotators are shown an agent query, the corresponding synthetic document generated by our pipeline, and the supporting context associated with the original question from HotpotQA or BrowseComp-Plus. They are then asked to independently judge whether the document appears trustworthy, whether its claims are factually correct (in this setting, relevance is always annotated as True). We run this annotation process in LabelStudio8 on 50 randomly selected tool calls. Three annotators are involved, and each document is annotated by at least 2 annotators, resulting in 100 annotations. In Table 2, we report raw accuracy and the binary correlation coefficient ϕ, and Cohens κ for interannotator agreement. Overall, the annotations show strong accuracy with respect to the intended synthetic labels and high inter-annotator agreement. Agreement is highest for trustworthiness, while factuality is more challenging, reflecting the greater ambiguity of judging whether all claims in generated document are correct. Further analysis in table 3 revealed that annotators tended to judge supposedly factual documents as non-factual, while supposedly non-factual documents were nearly always assessed as so. Evaluating factuality might require finer-grained assessment as some documents may be only partially correct, but overall, this evaluation confirms that our synthetic generation pipeline is consistent.

sections.title: B Aggregate metrics discussion
sections.content: In Section 3.4, we describe the Tokens Per Correctness (TPC) metric from Xie et al. (2026) and introduce our reliability-aware metrics: ReliabilityAware Score (RAS) and Cost per RAS (CoPRAS). These aggregate metrics depend on several design choices, including how correctness and cost are defined, and how the maximum tool-call budget is set. In this section, we discuss the motivation for these choices and illustrate their impact empirically. B.1 Design choices Cost. To make our results comparable with prior work, we reuse the cost definition from Xie et al. (2026), which combines generated tokens, input tokens, and the number of search calls. Following their setup, generated tokens have weight 1, input tokens have weight 0.25, and each search call has weight 500. These values are motivated by the relative cost of input and output tokens, and by the estimated cost of web-search API call expressed in equivalent output tokens. This choice is reasonable for web-search agents, but it is not universal. In particular, systems that search over local document collection, or use cheaper internal retriever rather than public search API, would require different weights. We therefore treat this cost function as useful reference point rather than an absolute measure of computational cost. 11 Figure 3: Human evaluation in our LabelStudio interface Scoring. Aggregate scores are useful because they allow us to rank systems directly. However, they also compress several different outcomes into single number. This choice is not neutral: it depends on what we want to evaluate. From user perspective, it may be enough that the system avoids giving wrong answer. From systemdesign perspective, we may want to distinguish more carefully between model that says dont know, model that keeps searching until the tool budget is exhausted, model that fails to produce valid answer tag, and model that gives an incorrect answer. RAS defines one possible scoring choice. It gives full credit to correct answers, no credit to incorrect or malformed answers, and partial credit to abstention or tool-budget exhaustion when reliable evidence is unlikely. This reflects the idea that, under degraded document conditions, not answering can be better than giving an unsupported answer. However, this is not the only possible design. For example, one could give less credit to tool-budget exhaustion than to explicit abstention, such as 0.5 ργi instead of 1 ργi, because clearly stating uncertainty may be preferable to searching until the budget is reached. This weighting is necessarily design choice. CoPRAS partly captures this difference through cost, since long searches are more expensive than early abstention. We therefore treat RAS and CoPRAS as summary metrics, not as replacements for the detailed outcome distributions. They are useful for comparing systems from reliability-oriented perspective, but other scoring choices could emphasize different behaviors. B.2 Impact of tool-call budget For the main experiments, we set the tool-call budget to 100. This choice directly affects our aggregate metrics. lower budget penalizes systems that usually need many searches before answering, since they are more likely to stop before producing final answer. It also affects cost-based metrics, because the number of tool calls is part of the cost definition. Changing the budget can therefore change both metric values and system rankings. We analyze this effect by recomputing the metrics under different tool-call budgets. Figure 4 shows how final-answer outcomes change as the budget increases. Figure 5 shows the corresponding evolution of Correctness, RAS, TPC, and CoPRAS. Overall, correctness increases with the budget, but the rate of improvement differs across systems. Models with narrow tool-call distributions reach their final performance quickly, while models with more spread-out distributions, such as GPT-5-nano (high) and GPT-5-mini (high), improve more gradually. As result, correctnessbased rankings become reasonably stable only after around 50 tool calls, although high-reasoning models continue to benefit from larger budgets. sections.title: C Additional qualitative experiments
sections.content: We report additional experiments that complement the main results with more qualitative view of agent behavior. We first examine the volume and content of search queries produced by different systems, and whether these queries change under degraded document conditions. We then analyze the agents reasoning steps to measure whether they explicitly identify low trustworthiness, low relevance, or low factuality of the returned documents in their chain-of-thoughts. These experiments are intended as exploratory process-level analyses and point to future work on more systematic evaluation of search-agent behavior beyond final-answer accuracy. C.1 Search queries C.1.1 Number of searches As shown in Figure 6, we observe large differences in the number of tool calls made by each agent. Since our setup exposes only one tool, search, this is equivalent to the number of search queries issued by the agent. Most specialized open-weight models make few tool calls, with limited variation as document quality decreases. The main exceptions are DR-Tulu, and SpiqaDR and Search-R1 when relevance is set to 0 on HotpotQA. GPT-based agents show clearer scaling with reasoning effort: low-effort runs are often close to open-weight models, while high-effort runs search much more extensively. For these models, document degradation generally increases the number of searches, especially at higher reasoning effort. 13 Figure 4: Detailed outcomes vs tool-calls budget Agents also search more on BrowseComp-Plus than on HotpotQA on average. This may reflect the role of parametric knowledge in HotpotQA, It may which can reduce the need for search. also reflect task structure: BrowseComp-Plus questions require persistent search over multiple constraints, whereas HotpotQA questions usually involve shorter multi-hop reasoning over Wikipediastyle facts. C.1.2 Queries content Agents also differ in how they adapt the content of their search queries under degraded document conditions. We track three query-level strategies that reflect increasingly constrained or source-aware search behavior: Exact-Match Operator: the query contains quoted text, indicating that the agent searches for an exact entity name, phrase, or clue span. Specify Source: the query targets particular source, domain, or source family, for example using site: operators or naming resources such as Wikipedia, IMDb, news outlets, archives, or domain-specific databases. Authority Cues: the query explicitly seeks authoritative evidence, for example by using terms such as official or reliable source, or by targeting institutional domains such as government or university websites. Figure 9 shows how often these strategies appear as document quality varies. We observe substantial differences across systems and degraded dimensions. First, systems differ strongly in their use of 14 (a) Correctness score evolution (b) Correctness rankings evolution (c) RAS score evolution (d) RAS rankings evolution (e) TPC score evolution (f) TPC rankings evolution (g) CoPRAS score evolution (h) CoPRAS rankings evolution Figure 5: Effect of tool budget on aggregate metrics: correctness, RAS, TPC, and CoPRAS. 15 (a) HotpotQA (b) BrowseComp-Plus Figure 6: Mean number of tool calls per dataset, per model, for values at 0%, 50% and 100% on all axes. exact-match operators, even when document quality is 100%. Some agents almost never use quoted queries, such as SpiqaDR. This is consistent with its training setup, where search is based on densevector retrieval rather than keyword search operators. By contrast, ASearcher and gpt-5-minibased agents use exact-match queries much more frequently. gpt-5-nano behaves differently: it uses exact-match operators in only about 30% of queries under perfect document conditions, but increases this rate to about 50% when relevance is degraded to 0%. This suggests that some agents respond to irrelevant results by making their queries more constrained. Second, trustworthiness degradation leads some agents to issue more source-aware queries. GPTbased systems and DR-Tulu more often specify specific source or domain when trustworthiness is low, suggesting that they try to redirect search toward more credible sources. We observe similar, though weaker, pattern for authority cues: these systems slightly increase the use of terms such as official or reliable source under low-trust conditions. Interestingly, degrading relevance has the opposite effect for the same systems, reducing the use of source-specific queries. This suggests that agents adapt differently depending on the perceived failure mode: low trustworthiness encourages source verification, whereas low relevance encourages query reformulation around the target content. Overall, query-content features reveal processlevel differences that are not visible from final answers alone. Some agents react to degraded documents by making queries more constrained or more source-aware, while others show little adaptation. These results are exploratory, but they suggest that query reformulation is an important component of robust search-agent behavior. C.2 Verbalization of degradation We also measure whether agents explicitly notice document degradation in their available reasoning traces. We use an LLM-as-a-judge to detect whether each reasoning step verbalizes concern about trustworthiness, relevance, or factuality. Since GPT-based agents expose only summaries of their internal reasoning, while open-weight agents expose full reasoning traces, comparisons between these families should be interpreted with caution. The evaluation prompt and hyperparameter details are provided in Appendix E. Applying this analysis to all reasoning steps would be costly, as our traces contain 335,274 steps in total. We therefore randomly sample 100 reasoning steps per system, scenario, and dataset, for total of 15,400 steps. We do not restrict samples to steps that immediately follow degraded document, so the resulting rate measures how often degradation concerns appear in traces, rather than direct reaction to each retrieved document. Figure 10 shows large differences across systems 16 and degradation axes. Search-R1 and AutoRefine almost never verbalize concerns about document quality. SpiqaDR and ASearcher mostly verbalize relevance issues, while rarely mentioning trustworthiness or factuality. This effect is especially strong for SpiqaDR: when relevance is set to 0%, it flags irrelevant documents in nearly 80% of sampled steps on BrowseComp-Plus and nearly 100% on HotpotQA. Among GPT-based agents, verbalization generally increases with reasoning effort for GPT-5-nano, although the pattern is less clear for GPT-5-mini. Across datasets, the difference between degraded and non-degraded conditions is smaller on BrowseComp-Plus than on HotpotQA. One possible explanation is that HotpotQA facts are more often available in parametric knowledge, making contradictions or irrelevant evidence easier for the model to detect. However, verbalization does not clearly translate into better final answers. In particular, removing explicit reasoning from DR-Tulu changes its interaction pattern, including the number of turns, and shifts its failures from format errors toward confident incorrect answers (cf. Section 5.1), but does not substantially change finalanswer correctness.

sections.content: D.1 Synthetic document generation D.1.1 Dynamic system prompt This section reports the prompt used to generate synthetic documents in our simulator. The prompt contains fixed instructions for query handling and output formatting, together with four dynamic placeholders. These placeholders are filled according to the sampled document attributes for the current search call: source trustworthiness, document relevance, and factuality. Colors indicate which attribute each placeholder controls: blue for source trustworthiness and orange for factuality and evidence grounding. Prompt for synthetic document generation. You are search engine simulator. Your goal is to generate plausible factuality_label documents, formatted in way that would look like it came from the first paragraph of the following source_quality website: {website_url} --- Query handling: - Only address what is explicitly asked in the query - Do not include information that would help answer the broader question below but wasn't requested - Treat the user message as the search query, even if it is long, broad, underspecified, or written as full natural-language question - Never ask the user for more specific query or for clarification. Always generate the synthetic document using the available context and the query as written Example: - Full question: "What is the spot on the second biggest planet of the solar system called?" - Query: "second biggest planet of the solar system" - Your answer should describe the planet, but must NOT mention the spot. Broader question the model is trying to answer: "{question}" source_style evidence_instructions --- Formatting examples: Bad output: **Bradley Cooper** (born January 5, 1975) is... Bad output: [Source](https://example.com) Bad output: Please provide specific query. Bad output: need more information to generate document. Good output: Bradley Cooper is an American actor and filmmaker known for performances in comedy, drama, and biographical films. He studied acting before moving into television and film, later becoming known for major studio releases and critically praised roles. His career includes acting, directing, producing, and voice work, with recognition from major film awards. Follow the good output style: one plain paragraph, no Markdown, no title line, no URLs, no refusals, no clarification requests, no meta-commentary, 80-140 words. --- You will now generate new synthetic document. The reward combines three signals: retrieval, answer quality, and format compliance. The retrieval component rewards the model for finding reference papers associated with the question. The answer-quality component is computed with METEOR between the generated final report and the reference answer. Finally, the format component enforces the expected agent protocol: the model must use valid tool calls and produce final answer after the tool responses. The final reward is the product of these components: = Rretrieval Rmeteor Rformat. This product form makes the reward strict: the model must retrieve relevant papers, produce an answer close to the reference, and follow the expected tool-use format. In practice, this was useful because optimizing only answer similarity did not reliably induce search behavior, while optimizing only retrieval did not produce useful final reports. D.3 Training details about SpiqaDR SpiqaDR is search-agent fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct for deep-research-style question answering over scientific literature, using agentic reinforcement learning with verl. The checkpoint is released in the HuggingFace catalog15 for reproducibility. SPIQA-derived training data. The training data is derived from the SPIQA (Pramanick et al., 2024) collection of machine-learning papers, from which the model takes its name. We start from the raw paper texts and enrich them with Semantic Scholar metadata using arXiv identifiers, including titles, authors, venues, years, abstracts, citations, and references. Our clustering procedure is inspired by the citation-graph community detection approach used in MDA-QA (Huang et al., 2025), but we adapt the graph construction and filtering criteria to our setting. We build an undirected graph where papers are nodes, and edges connect papers that cite or reference each other within our corpus. We then apply SLPA community detection with 50 iterations and filtering threshold of 0.1, and keep only communities containing 2 to 10 papers. This removes isolated papers, which cannot support multidocument questions, and overly large communities, which can exceed the context budget used for generation. For each selected community, we generate long-form QA example with GPT-4.1. The prompt provides the full text of all papers in the community and asks the model to identify facts specific to each document before generating an overarching question that requires information from all documents. The output contains the question, detailed answer with sources, and document-level annotations describing each papers contribution. The final dataset contains 1,000 examples, split into 800 training, 100 validation, and 100 test examples. Search environment.
